current_example.title: Example: Proving the Matrix Exponential Formula for IVP Solution of an Inhomogeneous System

q-334924.name: Question 1
q-334924.problem:
$$ {x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}]x+[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,x(1)=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] $$ Write down the expression that gives the solution of the initial value problem above. *Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}].$*
$x(t)=\,\,$ $3\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-1))+\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-1))$ $\,\,+{\int }_{1}^{t}\,\,$ {{field-1}} $\,\,\text{d}s$
{{field-2}} ${e}^{2s}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s))$
q-334924.worked_solution:
Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-1)}\,x(1) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-1)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-1)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-1)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-1))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-1))+\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-1)) \\ 3\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-1))+\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-1))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{e}^{2s} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2s}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ {e}^{2s}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-1))+\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-1)) \\ 3\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-1))+\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-1))\end{aligned}]+{\int }_{1}^{t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2s}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ {e}^{2s}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}]\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

$$ {x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ -4 & 0\end{aligned}]x+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ {e}^{4t}\end{aligned}],\,x(1)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 5\end{aligned}] $$ Write down the expression that gives the solution of the initial value problem above. *Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ -4 & 0\end{aligned}].$*

{{field-2}} ${e}^{4s}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s))$
q-334927.worked_solution:
Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}].$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-1)}\,x(1) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-1)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-1)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-1)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-1))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-1)) \\ 5\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-1))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s))\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ {e}^{4s}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4s}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ {e}^{4s}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}5\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-1)) \\ 5\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-1))\end{aligned}]+{\int }_{1}^{t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4s}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ {e}^{4s}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s))\end{aligned}]\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

x′(t)=[0440]x+[0e4t],x(0)=[13] Write down the expression that gives the solution of the initial value problem above.

Hint: eAt=[cosh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)cosh⁡(4t)], where A=[0440].

x(t)= cosh⁡(4t)+3sinh⁡(4t) +∫0t e4ssinh⁡(4(t−s)) ds

EXPLANATION

Given the system x′(t)=Ax(t)+g(t), where A is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution: x(t)=eA(t−t0)x(t0)⏟homogeneous part+∫t0teA(t−s)g(s)ds⏟particular solution, where x(t0) is the initial condition vector.

Let's evaluate each part separately:

  • First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that eAt=[cosh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)cosh⁡(4t)]. So, eAtx(0)=[cosh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)cosh⁡(4t)][13]=[cosh⁡(4t)+3sinh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)+3cosh⁡(4t)].

  • Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that eA(t−s)=[cosh⁡(4(t−s))sinh⁡(4(t−s))sinh⁡(4(t−s))cosh⁡(4(t−s))]. So, we have eA(t−s)g(s)=[cosh⁡(4(t−s))sinh⁡(4(t−s))sinh⁡(4(t−s))cosh⁡(4(t−s))][0e4s]=[e4ssinh⁡(4(t−s))e4scosh⁡(4(t−s))].

Therefore, we get x(t)=[cosh⁡(4t)+3sinh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)+3cosh⁡(4t)]+∫0t[e4ssinh⁡(4(t−s))e4scosh⁡(4(t−s))]ds.

q-334824.name: Question 5
q-334824.problem:
$$ {x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]x+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ {e}^{3t}\end{aligned}],\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] $$ Write down the expression that gives the solution of the initial value problem above. *Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} & t{e}^{3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{3t}\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}].$*
$x(t)=\,\,$ {{field-1}} $\,\,+{\int }_{0}^{t}\,\,$ $(t-s){e}^{3t}$ $\,\,\text{d}s$
$0$ {{field-2}}
q-334824.worked_solution:
Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} & t{e}^{3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{3t}\end{aligned}].$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At}\,x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} & t{e}^{3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{3t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{3(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{3(t-s)}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{3(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{3(t-s)}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ {e}^{3s}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(t-s){e}^{3t} \\ {e}^{3t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$

q-335088.name: Question 6
q-335088.problem:
$$ \{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=3y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=3x(t)+3,\end{aligned}\,[\begin{aligned}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] $$ Find the solution to the initial value problem above. *Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}].$*
$[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]=\,\,$ {{field-1}}
$\operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t)$
q-335088.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $g(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(3(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(3(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(3(t-s))\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(3(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(3(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(3(t-s))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sinh}⁡(3(t-s)) \\ 3\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3(t-s))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sinh}⁡(3(t-s)) \\ 3\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3(t-s))\end{aligned}]\text{d}s \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(3(t-s))\end{aligned}]}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t)-1 \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t)-1 \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t)-1 \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?
{x′(t)=y(t)+1y′(t)=x(t),[x(0)y(0)]=[00] Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

Hint: eAt=[cosh⁡(t)sinh⁡(t)sinh⁡(t)cosh⁡(t)], where A=[0110].

[x(t)y(t)]=
cosh⁡(t)
cosh⁡(t)
2sinh⁡(t)
sinh⁡(t)
2cosh⁡(t)
cosh⁡(t)−1
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Writing our system in matrix form, we get x′(t)=[0110]x(t)+g(t), where x(t)=[x(t)y(t)] and g(t)=[10]. So, the matrix of the system is A=[0110].

Given the system x′(t)=Ax(t)+g(t), where A is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution: x(t)=eA(t−t0)x(t0)⏟homogeneous part+∫t0teA(t−s)g(s)ds⏟particular solution, where x(t0) is the initial condition vector.

Let's evaluate each part separately:

  • First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that eAt=[cosh⁡(t)sinh⁡(t)sinh⁡(t)cosh⁡(t)]. Since the initial conditions are given at t=t0=0, we have eA(t−t0)=eAtx(0)=[cosh⁡(t)sinh⁡(t)sinh⁡(t)cosh⁡(t)][00]=[00].

  • Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that eA(t−s)=[cosh⁡(t−s)sinh⁡(t−s)sinh⁡(t−s)cosh⁡(t−s)]. So, we have eA(t−s)g(s)=[cosh⁡(t−s)sinh⁡(t−s)sinh⁡(t−s)cosh⁡(t−s)][10]=[cosh⁡(t−s)sinh⁡(t−s)]. Thus, we obtain ∫0teA(t−s)g(s)ds=∫0t[cosh⁡(t−s)sinh⁡(t−s)]ds=[−sinh⁡(t−s)−cosh⁡(t−s)]s=0s=t=[sinh⁡(t)cosh⁡(t)−1].

Finally, we get x(t)=[00]+[sinh⁡(t)cosh⁡(t)−1]=[sinh⁡(t)cosh⁡(t)−1].

q-334531.name: Question 8
q-334531.problem:
$$ \{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=2y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-2x(t)+1,\end{aligned}\,[\begin{aligned}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] $$ Find the solution to the initial value problem above. *Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}].$*
$[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}\,\,$ {{field-1}}
$3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)$
q-334531.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $g(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}]\text{d}s \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}]}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8
?
{x′(t)=2y(t)y′(t)=−2x(t)+1,[x(0)y(0)]=[−10] Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

Hint: eAt=[cos⁡(2t)sin⁡(2t)−sin⁡(2t)cos⁡(2t)], where A=[02−20].

[x(t)y(t)]=12
1−3cos(2t)
3sin⁡(2t)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Writing our system in matrix form, we get x′(t)=[02−20]x(t)+g(t), where x(t)=[x(t)y(t)] and g(t)=[01]. So, the matrix of the system is A=[02−20].

Given the system x′(t)=Ax(t)+g(t), where A is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution: x(t)=eA(t−t0)x(t0)⏟homogeneous part+∫t0teA(t−s)g(s)ds⏟particular solution, where x(t0) is the initial condition vector.

Let's evaluate each part separately:

  • First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that eAt=[cos⁡(2t)sin⁡(2t)−sin⁡(2t)cos⁡(2t)]. Since the initial conditions are given at t=t0=0, we have eA(t−t0)=eAtx(0)=[cos⁡(2t)sin⁡(2t)−sin⁡(2t)cos⁡(2t)][−10]=[−cos⁡(2t)sin⁡(2t)].

  • Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that eA(t−s)=[cos⁡(2(t−s))sin⁡(2(t−s))−sin⁡(2(t−s))cos⁡(2(t−s))]. So, we have eA(t−s)g(s)=[cos⁡(2(t−s))sin⁡(2(t−s))−sin⁡(2(t−s))cos⁡(2(t−s))][01]=[sin⁡(2(t−s))cos⁡(2(t−s))]. Thus, we obtain ∫0teA(t−s)g(s)ds=∫0t[sin⁡(2(t−s))cos⁡(2(t−s))]ds=[12cos⁡(2(t−s))−12sin⁡(2(t−s))]s=0s=t=12[1−cos⁡(2t)sin⁡(2t)].

Finally, we get x(t)=[−cos⁡(2t)sin⁡(2t)]+12[1−cos⁡(2t)sin⁡(2t)]=12[1−3cos⁡(2t)3sin⁡(2t)].

q-335183.name: Question 9
q-335183.problem:
$$ \{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=7y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=7x(t)+7,\end{aligned}\,[\begin{aligned}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] $$ Find the solution to the initial value problem above. *Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(7t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(7t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(7t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(7t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 7 \\ 7 & 0\end{aligned}].$*
$[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]=\,\,$ {{field-1}}
$\operatorname{sinh}⁡(7t)$
q-335183.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 7 \\ 7 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $g(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 7\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 7 \\ 7 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(7t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(7t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(7t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(7t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(7t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(7t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(7t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(7t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(7(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(7(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(7(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(7(t-s))\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(7(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(7(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(7(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(7(t-s))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7\operatorname{sinh}⁡(7(t-s)) \\ 7\operatorname{cosh}⁡(7(t-s))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}7\operatorname{sinh}⁡(7(t-s)) \\ 7\operatorname{cosh}⁡(7(t-s))\end{aligned}]\text{d}s \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{cosh}⁡(7(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(7(t-s))\end{aligned}]}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(7t)-1 \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(7t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(7t)-1 \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(7t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(7t)-1 \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(7t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

q-335085.name: Question 10
q-335085.problem:
$$ \{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=5x(t)+y(t)+1 \\ {y}^{′}(t)=5y(t),\end{aligned}\,[\begin{aligned}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] $$ Find the solution to the initial value problem above. *Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{5t} & t{e}^{5t} \\ 0 & {e}^{5t}\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}].$*
$[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{5}\,\,$ {{field-1}}
$0$
q-335085.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}]x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $g(t)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{5t} & t{e}^{5t} \\ 0 & {e}^{5t}\end{aligned}].
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x(0) & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{5t} & t{e}^{5t} \\ 0 & {e}^{5t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{5(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{5(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{5(t-s)}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{5(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{5(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{5(t-s)}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{5(t-s)} \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{5(t-s)} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\text{d}s \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{5}{e}^{5(t-s)} \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}{e}^{5t}-\frac{1}{5} \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}{e}^{5t}-\frac{1}{5} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}{e}^{5t}-\frac{1}{5} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{5t}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

q-335424.name: Question 11
q-335424.problem:
Consider the inhomogeneous system  ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x({t}_{0})$ is presented below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let $y(t)={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)$  

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}{x}^{′}(t)$  

$\text{L3}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t)$  

$\text{L4}:\,$ $y(t)-y({t}_{0})={\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $y({t}_{0})=x({t}_{0})$ 

$\text{L6}:\,$ $y(t)=x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s$  

$\text{L7}:\,$ ${e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t)=x(t)$

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ by  
{{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by  
{{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by  
{{field-3}}.
q-335424.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Integrating ${y}^{′}(t)={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t)$ from ${t}_{0}$ to $t$ in $\text{L3}$ yields

$$
y(t)-y({t}_{0})={\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Thus, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ by $\text{integrating both sides from }{t}_{0}\text{ to }t.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L5}.$ Evaluating $y(t)={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)$ at $t={t}_{0}$ gives

$$
y({t}_{0})={e}^{-A({t}_{0}-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})=Ix({t}_{0})=x({t}_{0}).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by $\text{evaluating at }t={t}_{0}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L8}.$ Multiplying both sides of

$$
y(t)={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)
$$

from $\text{L1}$ by ${e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t) & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t) \\  & =x(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by $\text{multiplying both sides by }{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}.$

q-335424.html:
Question 11
?
Consider the inhomogeneous system x′(t)=Ax(t)+g(t), where A is a constant square matrix. A derivation of the formula for the solution x(t) passing through x(t0) is presented below.

L1: Let y(t)=e−A(t−t0)x(t)

L2: y′(t)=−Ae−A(t−t0)x(t)+e−A(t−t0)x′(t)

L3: y′(t)=e−A(t−t0)g(t)

L4: y(t)−y(t0)=∫t0te−A(s−t0)g(s)ds

L5: y(t0)=x(t0)

L6: y(t)=x(t0)+∫t0te−A(s−t0)g(s)ds

L7: eA(t−t0)y(t)=eA(t−t0)x(t0)+∫t0teA(t−s)g(s)ds

L8: eA(t−t0)y(t)=x(t)

L9: x(t)=eA(t−t0)x(t0)+∫t0teA(t−s)g(s)ds

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

Line L4 follows from L3 by
integrating both sides from t0 to t
applying a change of variables
evaluating at t=t0
multiplying both sides by eA(t−t0)
integrating both sides from t0 to t
.

Line L5 follows from line L1 by
evaluating at t=t0
multiplying both sides by eA(t−t0)
differentiating and using the sum rule
multiplying both sides by eA(t+t0)
evaluating at t=t0
.

Line L8 follows from line L1 by
multiplying both sides by eA(t−t0)
multiplying both sides by eA(t+t0)
evaluating at t=t0
differentiating and using the sum rule
multiplying both sides by eA(t−t0)
.
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's justify each of the selected steps.

  • We first consider lines L3 and L4. Integrating y′(t)=e−A(t−t0)g(t) from t0 to t in L3 yields
    y(t)−y(t0)=∫t0te−A(s−t0)g(s)ds.
    Thus, L4 follows from L3 by integrating both sides from t0 to t.

  • Next, we consider lines L1 and L5. Evaluating y(t)=e−A(t−t0)x(t) at t=t0 gives
    y(t0)=e−A(t0−t0)x(t0)=Ix(t0)=x(t0). Therefore, L5 follows from L1 by evaluating at t=t0.

  • Finally, we consider lines L1 and L8. Multiplying both sides of y(t)=e−A(t−t0)x(t) from L1 by eA(t−t0) gives
    eA(t−t0)y(t)=eA(t−t0)e−A(t−t0)x(t)=x(t). Therefore, L8 follows from L1 by multiplying both sides by eA(t−t0).

q-335422.name: Question 12
q-335422.problem:
Consider the inhomogeneous system  ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x({t}_{0})$ is presented below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let $y(t)={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)$  

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}{x}^{′}(t)$  

$\text{L3}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t)$  

$\text{L4}:\,$ $y(t)-y({t}_{0})={\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $y({t}_{0})=x({t}_{0})$ 

$\text{L6}:\,$ $y(t)=x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s$  

$\text{L7}:\,$ ${e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t)=x(t)$

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by  
{{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line
{{field-2}}
by substituting 
{{field-3}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by  
{{field-4}}.
q-335422.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Differentiating $y(t)={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)$ and applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =({e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})})^{′}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}{x}^{′}(t) \\  & =(-A){e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}{x}^{′}(t) \\  & =-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}{x}^{′}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by $\text{differentiating and using the product rule}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L4}$, $\text{L5}$, and $\text{L6}.$ From $\text{L4}$ we have

$$
y(t)-y({t}_{0})={\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Using $y({t}_{0})=x({t}_{0})$ from $\text{L5}$, this becomes

$$
y(t)-x({t}_{0})={\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s,
$$

so

$$
y(t)=x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Thus, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L4}$ by substituting $y({t}_{0})=x({t}_{0}).$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ Multiplying both sides of

$$
y(t)=x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,ds
$$

from $\text{L6}$ by ${e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t) & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L7}$ follows from $\text{L6}$ by $\text{multiplying both sides by }{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}.$

Consider the inhomogeneous system x′(t)=Ax(t)+g(t), where A is a constant square matrix. A derivation of the formula for the solution x(t) passing through x(t0) is presented below.

L1: Let y(t)=e−A(t−t0)x(t)

L2: y′(t)=−Ae−A(t−t0)x(t)+e−A(t−t0)x′(t)

L3: y′(t)=e−A(t−t0)g(t)

L4: y(t)−y(t0)=∫t0te−A(s−t0)g(s)ds

L5: y(t0)=x(t0)

L6: y(t)=x(t0)+∫t0te−A(s−t0)g(s)ds

L7: eA(t−t0)y(t)=eA(t−t0)x(t0)+∫t0teA(t−s)g(s)ds

L8: eA(t−t0)y(t)=x(t)

L9: x(t)=eA(t−t0)x(t0)+∫t0teA(t−s)g(s)ds

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

EXPLANATION

Let's justify each of the selected steps.

  • We first consider lines L1 and L2. Differentiating y(t)=e−A(t−t0)x(t) and applying the product rule gives
    y′(t)=(e−A(t−t0))′x(t)+e−A(t−t0)x′(t)=(−A)e−A(t−t0)x(t)+e−A(t−t0)x′(t)=−Ae−A(t−t0)x(t)+e−A(t−t0)x′(t). Thus, L2 follows from L1 by differentiating and using the product rule.

  • Next, we consider lines L4, L5, and L6. From L4 we have y(t)−y(t0)=∫t0te−A(s−t0)g(s)ds. Using y(t0)=x(t0) from L5, this becomes
    y(t)−x(t0)=∫t0te−A(s−t0)g(s)ds, so y(t)=x(t0)+∫t0te−A(s−t0)g(s)ds. Thus, L6 follows from L4 by substituting y(t0)=x(t0).

  • Finally, we consider lines L6 and L7. Multiplying both sides of y(t)=x(t0)+∫t0te−A(s−t0)g(s)ds from L6 by eA(t−t0) gives

q-335425.problem:
Consider the inhomogeneous system  ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x({t}_{0})$ is presented below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let $y(t)={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)$  

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}{x}^{′}(t)$  

$\text{L3}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t)$  

$\text{L4}:\,$ $y(t)-y({t}_{0})={\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $y({t}_{0})=x({t}_{0})$ 

$\text{L6}:\,$ $y(t)=x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s$  

$\text{L7}:\,$ ${e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t)=x(t)$

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by  
{{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line
{{field-2}}
by substituting 
{{field-3}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L9}$ follows from line $\text{L7}$ by  
{{field-4}}.
q-335425.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Differentiating $y(t)={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)$ and applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =({e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})})^{′}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}{x}^{′}(t) \\  & =(-A){e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}{x}^{′}(t) \\  & =-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}{x}^{′}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by $\text{differentiating and using the product rule}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L4}$, $\text{L5}$, and $\text{L6}.$ From $\text{L4}$ we have

$$
y(t)-y({t}_{0})={\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Using $y({t}_{0})=x({t}_{0})$ from $\text{L5}$, this becomes

$$
y(t)-x({t}_{0})={\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s,
$$

so

$$
y(t)=x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Thus, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L4}$ by substituting $y({t}_{0})=x({t}_{0}).$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L7}$, $\text{L8}$, and $\text{L9}.$ From $\text{L8}$ we know that

$$
{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t)=x(t).
$$

Substituting ${e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t)=x(t)$ into

$$
{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s
$$

from $\text{L7}$ gives

$$
x(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Therefore, $\text{L9}$ follows from $\text{L7}$ by $\text{substituting }{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t)=x(t).$

q-335425.html:
Question 13
?
Consider the inhomogeneous system x′(t)=Ax(t)+g(t), where A is a constant square matrix. A derivation of the formula for the solution x(t) passing through x(t0) is presented below.

L1: Let y(t)=e−A(t−t0)x(t)

L2: y′(t)=−Ae−A(t−t0)x(t)+e−A(t−t0)x′(t)

L3: y′(t)=e−A(t−t0)g(t)

L4: y(t)−y(t0)=∫t0te−A(s−t0)g(s)ds

L5: y(t0)=x(t0)

L6: y(t)=x(t0)+∫t0te−A(s−t0)g(s)ds

L7: eA(t−t0)y(t)=eA(t−t0)x(t0)+∫t0teA(t−s)g(s)ds

L8: eA(t−t0)y(t)=x(t)

L9: x(t)=eA(t−t0)x(t0)+∫t0teA(t−s)g(s)ds

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

Line L2 follows from L1 by
differentiating and using the product rule
substituting x′(t)=Ax(t)+g(t)+t0
evaluating at t=t0
applying a change of variables
differentiating and using the product rule
.

Line L6 follows from line
L4
L3
L4
L1
by substituting
y(t0)=x(t0)
y(t0)=x(t0)
x′(t)=Ax(t)+g(t)+t0
y(t)=e−A(t−t0)x(t)
eA(t−t0)y(t)=x(t)+t0
.

Line L9 follows from line L7 by
substituting eA(t−t0)y(t)=x(t)
evaluating at t=t0
multiplying both sides by eA(t−t0)
substituting eA(t−t0)y(t)=x(t)
substituting eA(t−t0)y(t)=x(t)+t0
.
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's justify each of the selected steps.

  • We first consider lines L1 and L2. Differentiating y(t)=e−A(t−t0)x(t) and applying the product rule gives
    y′(t)=(e−A(t−t0))′x(t)+e−A(t−t0)x′(t)=(−A)e−A(t−t0)x(t)+e−A(t−t0)x′(t)=−Ae−A(t−t0)x(t)+e−A(t−t0)x′(t). Thus, L2 follows from L1 by differentiating and using the product rule.

  • Next, we consider lines L4, L5, and L6. From L4 we have y(t)−y(t0)=∫t0te−A(s−t0)g(s)ds. Using y(t0)=x(t0) from L5, this becomes
    y(t)−x(t0)=∫t0te−A(s−t0)g(s)ds, so y(t)=x(t0)+∫t0te−A(s−t0)g(s)ds. Thus, L6 follows from L4 by substituting y(t0)=x(t0).

  • Finally, we consider lines L7, L8, and L9. From L8 we know that eA(t−t0)y(t)=x(t). Substituting eA(t−t0)y(t)=x(t) into eA(t−t0)y(t)=eA(t−t0)x(t0)+∫t0teA(t−s)g(s)ds from L7 gives
    x(t)=eA(t−t0)x(t0)+∫t0teA(t−s)g(s)ds. Therefore, L9 follows from L7 by substituting eA(t−t0)y(t)=x(t).

q-335431.problem:
Consider the inhomogeneous system  ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x({t}_{0})$ is presented below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let $y(t)={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)$  

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}{x}^{′}(t)$  

$\text{L3}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t)$  

$\text{L4}:\,$ $y(t)-y({t}_{0})={\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $y({t}_{0})=x({t}_{0})$ 

$\text{L6}:\,$ $y(t)=x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s$  

$\text{L7}:\,$ ${e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t)=x(t)$

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by  
{{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by  
{{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L9}$ follows from line $\text{L7}$ by  
{{field-3}}.
q-335431.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Differentiating $y(t)={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)$ and applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =({e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})})^{′}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}{x}^{′}(t) \\  & =(-A){e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}{x}^{′}(t) \\  & =-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}{x}^{′}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by $\text{differentiating and using the product rule}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ Multiplying both sides of

$$
y(t)=x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s
$$

from $\text{L6}$ by ${e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t) & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L7}$ follows from $\text{L6}$ by $\text{multiplying both sides by }{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L7}$, $\text{L8}$, and $\text{L9}.$ From $\text{L8}$ we know that

$$
{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t)=x(t).
$$

Substituting ${e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t)=x(t)$ into

$$
{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s
$$

from $\text{L7}$ gives

$$
x(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Therefore, $\text{L9}$ follows from $\text{L7}$ by $\text{substituting }{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t)=x(t).$

q-335431.html:
Question 14
?
Consider the inhomogeneous system x′(t)=Ax(t)+g(t), where A is a constant square matrix. A derivation of the formula for the solution x(t) passing through x(t0) is presented below.

L1: Let y(t)=e−A(t−t0)x(t)

L2: y′(t)=−Ae−A(t−t0)x(t)+e−A(t−t0)x′(t)

L3: y′(t)=e−A(t−t0)g(t)

L4: y(t)−y(t0)=∫t0te−A(s−t0)g(s)ds

L5: y(t0)=x(t0)

L6: y(t)=x(t0)+∫t0te−A(s−t0)g(s)ds

L7: eA(t−t0)y(t)=eA(t−t0)x(t0)+∫t0teA(t−s)g(s)ds

L8: eA(t−t0)y(t)=x(t)

L9: x(t)=eA(t−t0)x(t0)+∫t0teA(t−s)g(s)ds

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

Line L2 follows from L1 by
applying a change of variables
applying a change of variables
substituting x′(t)=Ax(t)+g(t)
substituting x′(t)=Ax(t)+g(t)+t0
differentiating and using the product rule
.

Line L7 follows from line L6 by
multiplying both sides by eA(t−t0)
evaluating at t=t0
multiplying both sides by eA(t+t0)
integrating both sides
multiplying both sides by eA(t−t0)
.

Line L9 follows from line L7 by
substituting eA(t−t0)y(t)=x(t)
evaluating at t=t0
multiplying both sides by eA(t−t0)
substituting eA(t+t0)y(t)=x(t)
substituting eA(t−t0)y(t)=x(t)
.
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let's justify each of the selected steps.

  • We first consider lines L1 and L2. Differentiating y(t)=e−A(t−t0)x(t) and applying the product rule gives
    y′(t)=(e−A(t−t0))′x(t)+e−A(t−t0)x′(t)=(−A)e−A(t−t0)x(t)+e−A(t−t0)x′(t)=−Ae−A(t−t0)x(t)+e−A(t−t0)x′(t). Thus, L2 follows from L1 by differentiating and using the product rule.

  • Next, we consider lines L6 and L7. Multiplying both sides of y(t)=x(t0)+∫t0te−A(s−t0)g(s)ds from L6 by eA(t−t0) gives
    eA(t−t0)y(t)=eA(t−t0)x(t0)+eA(t−t0)∫t0te−A(s−t0)g(s)ds=eA(t−t0)x(t0)+∫t0teA(t−s)g(s)ds. Therefore, L7 follows from L6 by multiplying both sides by eA(t−t0).

  • Finally, we consider lines L7, L8, and L9. From L8 we know that eA(t−t0)y(t)=x(t). Substituting eA(t−t0)y(t)=x(t) into eA(t−t0)y(t)=eA(t−t0)x(t0)+∫t0teA(t−s)g(s)ds from L7 gives
    x(t)=eA(t−t0)x(t0)+∫t0teA(t−s)g(s)ds. Therefore, L9 follows from L7 by substituting eA(t−t0)y(t)=x(t).

q-334533.name: Question 15
q-334533.problem:
Consider the inhomogeneous system  ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x(0)$ is presented below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let $y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)$  

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t)$  

$\text{L3}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)={e}^{-At}g(t)$  

$\text{L4}:\,$ $y(t)-y(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $y(0)=x(0)$ 

$\text{L6}:\,$ $y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$  

$\text{L7}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)=x(t)$

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Differentiating $y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)$ and applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =({e}^{-At})^{′}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t) \\  & =(-A){e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t) \\  & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by $\text{differentiating and using the product rule}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Integrating ${y}^{′}(t)={e}^{-At}g(t)$ from $0$ to $t$ in $\text{L3}$ yields

$$
y(t)-y(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

So, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ by integrating both sides from $0$ to $t.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ Multiplying both sides of

$$
y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,ds
$$

from $\text{L6}$ by ${e}^{At}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At}y(t) & ={e}^{At}x(0)+{e}^{At}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L7}$ follows from $\text{L6}$ by $\text{multiplying both sides by }{e}^{At}.$

    y′(t)=(e−At)′x(t)+e−Atx′(t)=(−A)e−Atx(t)+e−Atx′(t)=−Ae−Atx(t)+e−Atx′(t). Thus, L2 follows from L1 by differentiating and using the product rule.

  • Next, we consider lines L3 and L4. Integrating y′(t)=e−Atg(t) from 0 to t in L3 yields
    y(t)−y(0)=∫0te−Asg(s)ds.
    So, L4 follows from L3 by integrating both sides from 0 to t.

  • Finally, we consider lines L6 and L7. Multiplying both sides of y(t)=x(0)+∫0te−Asg(s)ds from L6 by eAt gives
    eAty(t)=eAtx(0)+eAt∫0te−Asg(s)ds=eAtx(0)+∫0teA(t−s)g(s)ds. Therefore, L7 follows from L6 by multiplying both sides by eAt.
